o: Count distinct three-digit even numbers formable from the given multiset of digits, no leading zero, each copy used once per number. With at most 10 digits, brute force over all ordered triples (a,b,c) checking frequency feasibility is trivially fast. Example 2 ([0,2,2]): valid numbers are 202 and 220 → 2. Example 3 ([6,6,6]): only 666 → 1. Example 4 (no even digits) → 0.
k: A number abc is formable iff digit counts suffice: cnt[a]>=1, cnt[b]>=1, cnt[c]>=1 accounting for repeats (e.g., a==b needs cnt>=2).
Enumerate hundreds digit a in 1..9, tens b in 0..9, units c in {0,2,4,6,8}.
Only 9*10*5 = 450 candidates, so no cleverness needed.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Candidates
a.i: Try every combination (a, b, c) with a != 0 and c even; verify the multiset of digits used is available in the input counts. Since there are at most 450 triples, this is instantaneous and obviously correct.
s: Build a count array of the input digits.
Triple loop over a in 1..9, b in 0..9, c in even digits.
Check counts: decrement needed copies per distinct digit and verify none go negative.
a.t: O(450 * 10) = O(1) — fixed number of candidate triples times digit-count check.

a.n: Approach 2: Generate Permutations Into a Set
a.i: Generate all permutations of the digits array (up to 10! = 3.6M, still acceptable), take the first three digits of each, and insert valid numbers into a set to deduplicate. Simpler to reason about but wasteful when digits repeat.
s: Use a permutations library on the full digits list.
For each permutation, form the number from the first three digits.
If it has no leading zero and is even, add it to a set.
a.t: O(P(10,3)) distinct-prefix permutations ≈ O(720) with dedup pruning; worst-case library version O(10!) but fine for n <= 10.
a.sp: O(1) — bounded output set size (at most 900 numbers).

w: Prefer Approach 1 in interviews: it's direct, provably correct, and constant time. Pitfalls: allowing leading zeros, forgetting repeated digits require multiple copies (e.g., 222 from a single 2), and double-counting duplicates like 202 appearing from different index orders. Follow-up: generalize to k-digit numbers or count numbers divisible by another value — the same frequency-check enumeration extends naturally.
